entry.title: Lucid Bought My Car Back, So I Bought A Mach-E

media:group.media:title: Lucid Bought My Car Back, So I Bought A Mach-E
media:group.media:description:
Lucid bought back my Air, so I bought a Ford Mustang Mach-E GT Check out Continental's ECS02 Tires! - https://bit.ly/3Ulidu1 Sponsored by Continental
Genuinely this was some of the most fun I’ve ever had car shopping because the criteria was very open: pretty much anything electric, except for three brands. I’ve already had a long term Nissan Leaf, I’ve had two Teslas, and technically I’ve had two Lucids. Lucid bought back my super finicky air, and so my plan was to replace it with the Rivian R2, but my build date still hasn’t come up, and the Lucid was going away, so I wanted something until I could get my Rivian.
But Lucid actually had this covered, as they offered me a long-term Gravity that I could use until the end of this year, at which point I’d probably get my Rivian order placed. But less than a week passed, before the Lucid Gravity’s window wouldn’t go up, even with multiple vehicle resets. Yes, the window on a brand new press car would only occasionally work. I sent the car back to service, and decided to cut my losses, because it was apparent Lucid and I are like water and oil. No matter how much you stir, it’s not gonna work out.
So while I wait for the Rivian order, I thought what the heck, I’ll buy a car that’s already taken it’s huge depreciation hit, and then sell it when I get the Rivian. And since the intent was just a short-term use, I wanted to try something different, so not a Nissan, not a Tesla, not a Lucid. I wanted something weird, something different. I just said that. That’s when I landed on the Genesis GV60 Performance in highlighter yellow-green. I think Genesis is making some of the best interiors in modern cars, regardless of price range, and I found one nearby. Well it sold the day I called the dealer about it, and it turns out not many people have as bad of visual taste as I do, so finding another highlighter GV60 Performance proved challenging.
That’s when I spotted this Mach-e GT Performance, in highlighter orange. This is a 2022 Mach-E, that I bought for almost exactly half of its MSRP, which was $73,290.00. Yes, a one-owner, perfectly clean, well maintained, 16,000 mile Mach-e with all the bells & whistles lost well over $35,000 in depreciation in just four years. Sounds like a great deal to me; I’m in.

entry.title: How To Easily Ruin Your Turbocharged Car

media:group.media:title: How To Easily Ruin Your Turbocharged Car
media:group.media:description:
If you want to ruin your turbocharged car, it’s easy. All you have to do is drive your car hard, then immediately shut it off. You see, turbos are one of the hottest parts of your car, since all of the exhaust gases are routed through it. To help enable high turbo speeds, and to help cool it, engine oil pass through the insides of the turbocharger, directly contacting the shaft connecting the compressor and turbine wheels. When you drive hard, this shaft, and the surrounding oil channel areas, get extremely hot. If you shut your engine off right after driving hard, the nearby oil just soaks in this heat, literally cooking it, and building up deposits on the turboshaft. To prevent this, it’s a good idea to start chilling out with your right foot when you start to get close to your destination, this way the turbo can cool down to more manageable temperatures before you shut your engine off.

entry.title: Bigger Brakes Won't Stop You Any Faster

media:group.media:title: Bigger Brakes Won't Stop You Any Faster
media:group.media:description:
If you had to choose between super powerful brakes or super sticky tires, which helps you stop faster? Brakes make you stop, so you might think brakes, but the real answer is tires. Any modern car already has enough force in the calipers to lock up a wheel. The limit on stopping distance isn't the brake, it's whatever grip the tire has with the road. Better tire, better braking. It’s really that simple. And with modern ABS, you just mash the pedal and get insanely good stopping distances. But if do that again, and again, and again, and excessive heat builds up in the brakes, your stopping distance fades. That's brake fade. For repeated hard stops, like on a track, upgrading brakes provides meaningful improvement in consistency.

entry.title: Porsche's 6-Stroke Engine Is Fascinating – More Power!

media:group.media:title: Porsche's 6-Stroke Engine Is Fascinating – More Power!
media:group.media:description:
Porsche patented a 6-stroke engine, yes, two more strokes than you’d commonly see for a combustion engine, and most excitingly, one of those additional strokes is a power-stroke! We now have two power strokes per cylinder within the full six-stroke cycle. The way it works is through Porsche’s genius hypocycloidal design which the crankshaft follows. This creates two different stopping heights for the piston at both the top, and the bottom of the cylinder. The first three strokes you’ve seen before, intake, compression, power, but at the end of our third stroke, the first power stroke, the piston drops a little bit further down, exposing air intake ports, filling the cylinder with fresh air. This is of course compressed on the next stroke, along with fuel, leading to the second power stroke, and finally ending with the exhaust stroke, before the cycle repeats. The advantage is greater power density, since you know have more frequent power strokes. The downside is, it’s just a patent, so much like my ambitions to learn how to read, it might not ever happen.

entry.title: Why Downshifting To Slow Down Is Actually Genius – Engine Braking!

media:group.media:title: Why Downshifting To Slow Down Is Actually Genius – Engine Braking!
media:group.media:description:
If you've ever driven a manual, you've experienced engine braking: the car actively slowing down when you lift off the throttle. But what's actually happening? With gasoline engines, when you lift off, the throttle valve nearly closes. Now, as the pistons hit their intake stroke, they're trying to pull air against that nearly closed valve, creating a vacuum. That resistance is the main factor slowing your car: the pistons are fighting to draw air through a tiny opening, which slows their motion. Slower pistons, slower engine, and since you're in gear, slower wheels. Engine braking! In a lower gear, like 2nd or 3rd, you slow even more, since the engine spins faster and pulls against that restricted throttle more frequently. And instead of your brakes absorbing the heat, your engine's cooling system handles it easily. It's nothing compared to the combustion heat it already deals with. That's why engine braking is so useful on long downhill stretches.

entry.title: Everyone Hates CVTs, but eCVTS are Genius!

media:group.media:title: Everyone Hates CVTs, but eCVTS are Genius!
media:group.media:description:
Everyone hates CVTs, or continuously variable transmissions. The reason is when they first started getting widely adopted, they used belts, which often suffered reliability problems, and they also didn’t feel great to drive. And while belt-CVTs have improved tremendously, there might be a better way. eCVTs do away with all the belts and pulleys, in favor of a single planetary gear set. When you pair this with an engine and two electric motors, you can generate basically any gear ratio you want for that engine, and it’s dead reliable and dead simple. Automatic transmissions typically use several of these planetary sets in combination for all the various gears, whereas an eCVT uses just the one. There’s a longer video explaining it all for those curious, and while it’s operation may feel complex, the beauty is truly how simple of a solution it is. Simplicity has always been beautiful, it’s why I’m proud my brain is completely smooth.

Ducati has a bit of a secret as far as how their engines rev so high, reaching 16,500 RPM from their 1.0L Desmosedici Stradale R V4 used in the Panigale R. You might already know they’re using a short piston stroke to maximize RPM, or that they use desmodromic valves, allowing for crazy high valve-train speeds. But there’s another trick up their sleeves, which stems from the fact that they’re using a 90-degree V4, but the crankshaft pins are separated by 70 degrees. Not a nice clean number like 0, 90, or 180 degrees, like you might see elsewhere, but 70 degrees. Why? Well in this video, the finale of three episodes on Ducati V4 engines, we will finally get to the bottom of it.

media:group.media:title: 4 Problems With Direct Injection Engines
media:group.media:description:
The single biggest technology change to gasoline combustion engines over the past 50 years is arguably direct fuel injection, and unfortunately, it brought with it problems. In 1975, over 95% of gasoline engines sold in America were carbureted. By the year 2000, nearly 100% of gas engines (99.8%) had made the switch to port injection. And by the year 2025, over 80% of gas engines are now using direct injection, thanks to the power and efficiency benefits. Most people are aware of the carbon deposit challenge that GDI engines face, since port-injectors no longer clean the intake valves. But there are three other challenges: soot formation, which in turn can cause wear on timing chains, fuel dilution, from DI engines directly spraying cylinder walls - especially for shorter trips, and LSPI, destructive behavior that stems from small, turbocharged engines making more power at low RPM, in part thanks to GDI. So while the industry initially seemed to be abandoning port-injection, it’s made a comeback, in combination with direct-injection.

entry.title: Ducati V4 Engines Are Different From Everything Else – Here’s Why

media:group.media:title: Ducati V4 Engines Are Different From Everything Else – Here’s Why
media:group.media:description:
Ducati’s V4 Engine Is Unlike Anything Else - Here’s Why They Do Things Differently! Subscribe to Engineering Explained for more videos! - https://goo.gl/VZstk7 Recommended Books & Car Products - http://amzn.to/2BrekJm
With four-cylinder engines, there are many great reasons to go with an inline layout, especially in cars. But in motorcycles, there are many great reasons to go with a V4 layout, as I’ve explained in my previous video on Ducati V4 engines. Once you’ve narrowed it down to a 90-degree V4, meaning two-cylinders on one bank, and two cylinders on another bank 90 degrees apart, there are three obvious options for your crankshaft (0º, 90º and 180º crank pin splits), which significantly change the characteristics of the engine. Which one does Ducati for their modern V4? None of them. Instead, they opt for a 70º crank pin split. It’s a seemingly bizarre choice, but it’s actually very smart, so in this video we’re going to explain why Ducati does it the way they do it.
This will also help answer the question why Ducati bikes sound so good, which of course is subjective, but there’s a real science behind that sound.
